title: The Fabian Strategy

jokes.text: - Lemon, it's Jack. - Who's Jackie?
jokes.setup: Jack calls Liz and announces himself formally as 'Jack'
jokes.punchline: Liz, clearly not paying attention or being deliberately obtuse, responds 'Who's Jackie?' — misidentifying him entirely
jokes.explanation: Classic cold-open Liz Lemon move — her distracted, deflating response to Jack's grandiose self-announcement. It establishes the dynamic economically and is true to her character, but it's a familiar bit of business for the show.

jokes.text: surf, sun, and... Sandwiches? Heh, we didn't need sandwiches, Lemon.
jokes.setup: Jack is listing the three 's's of his luxurious vacation: surf, sun, and...
jokes.punchline: Liz interrupts with 'Sandwiches?' — the most pedestrian possible third item — and Jack's dismissive correction ('we didn't need sandwiches') perfectly punctuates it
jokes.explanation: Brilliantly economical. Liz's food-obsessed brain completing Jack's luxury list with 'sandwiches' is perfectly character-integrated for both: Jack's aspirational speech deflated by Liz's plebeian instincts. His deadpan correction doubles the laugh. Two characters, one exchange, two big laughs — excellent structure.

jokes.text: It was so warm you could pick fully cooked lobsters out of the water.
jokes.setup: Jack is describing the idyllic vacation conditions
jokes.punchline: The absurd escalation that the water was so warm it literally cooked shellfish — delivered with complete sincerity
jokes.explanation: Effective absurdist escalation of Jack's vacation bragging — the hyperbole crosses into the surreal. The deadpan delivery is key. Solid but not exceptional.

jokes.text: Avery is the most perfect woman ever created. Like a young Bo Derek stuffed with a Barry Goldwater.
jokes.setup: Jack is effusively praising Avery as the ideal woman
jokes.punchline: The simile that completes the compliment: physical beauty (Bo Derek) fused with hardcore conservative ideology (Barry Goldwater) — a perfectly Donaghy-specific ideal woman
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's best jokes. 'Bo Derek stuffed with a Barry Goldwater' could only come from Jack Donaghy — it reveals his character (he finds conservative ideology as attractive as physical beauty) while being genuinely surprising and absurd. The verb 'stuffed' does enormous comic work. Highly quotable, completely character-specific, and original.

jokes.text: You sound weird. Do you have a beard?
jokes.setup: Jack has just been waxing rhapsodic about his perfect vacation
jokes.punchline: Liz's complete non-sequitur response focuses on whether he has a beard, cutting through his eloquence with mundane curiosity
jokes.explanation: Another Liz deflation of Jack's grand speech, this time with a banal non-sequitur. Functional, true to character, but a familiar move.

jokes.text: No more making love on the beach surrounded by a privacy circle of English-trained butlers.
jokes.setup: Jack is lamenting the end of his vacation luxury
jokes.punchline: The specific, absurdly opulent detail — not just butlers, but English-trained ones, forming a 'privacy circle' while he makes love on the beach — reveals the extreme specificity of Jack's wealthy fantasy life
jokes.explanation: The joke rewards attention: it's not just butlers (already funny), they're English-trained (specific comedy of implied superiority), and they form a 'privacy circle' (geometrically absurd). Each word earns its place. Deeply character-specific to Jack.

jokes.text: Get this, my gynecologist committed suicide. And I'm back!
jokes.setup: Jack asks how Liz's summer was, expecting a comparable story
jokes.punchline: Liz's summer highlight is her gynecologist's suicide — delivered with the energy of someone sharing good news, followed by 'And I'm back!' as if this constitutes a triumphant return
jokes.explanation: Near-perfect joke construction. The setup is Jack's breezy 'how was your summer,' the expected response is a counter-vacation story. Instead: something genuinely dark, totally specific to Liz's chaotic life, delivered as if it's a punchline to a good anecdote. 'And I'm back!' is the second punchline — triumphant energy about a terrible summer. The juxtaposition with Jack's idyllic vacation is the cherry on top.

jokes.text: No, wait, actually that's a half-burned-down McDonald's.
jokes.setup: Carol says he can see the arch from Lambert-St. Louis airport
jokes.punchline: Mid-sentence correction: it's not the iconic Gateway Arch, just a half-burned McDonald's (whose arch shape mirrors the Arch)
jokes.explanation: Clean, layered joke: the St. Louis arch confusion is well-trodden territory but 'half-burned-down' adds unexpected specificity that elevates it beyond the obvious McDonald's arches gag. The mid-sentence self-correction structure is tight.

jokes.text: St. Louis-Newark, Newark-Atlantic City, Atlantic City to Newark, and then I'll be there. Who flies Newark to Atlantic City? Black bachelorette parties. Gotta go.
jokes.setup: Carol rattles off his absurd connecting flight itinerary, ending with the bizarre leg Newark-Atlantic City
jokes.punchline: Liz's incredulous 'Who flies Newark to Atlantic City?' is immediately answered with Carol's oddly specific and confident 'Black bachelorette parties' — then he hangs up instantly
jokes.explanation: The joke's structure is excellent: itinerary establishes the absurdity, the Newark-AC leg invites the question, and the answer is hyper-specific and delivered with absolute zero hesitation. 'Gotta go' seals it — he has no time to explain. The abrupt hang-up is its own mini-punchline.

jokes.text: Oh, I misdialed. I thought I was calling my nutritionist. Good-bye.
jokes.setup: Tracy calls Liz enthusiastically promising 110% effort this season
jokes.punchline: He then reveals he dialed the wrong number entirely — the speech was for his nutritionist, not his boss — and hangs up without any acknowledgment
jokes.explanation: Excellent misdirection with perfect Tracy-specificity. The setup is a familiar trope (employee promises boss a great season), the punchline is that the whole speech was misdirected AND the content (110% effort, relaxed, focused) was for a nutritionist rather than for work — implying the nutritionist relationship is more demanding. Tracy's breezy goodbye completes it. Fully earns its score.

jokes.text: Okay, season five. Here we go.
jokes.setup: Liz has just survived a barrage of chaotic phone calls from her colleagues
jokes.punchline: Her resigned 'Okay, season five. Here we go.' directly acknowledges the show's own season premiere, breaking the fourth wall while expressing exhausted resignation
jokes.explanation: 30 Rock's meta-self-awareness is always well-deployed here. The joke works on two levels: Liz steeling herself for another season of chaos in-universe, and the show acknowledging its own fifth season premiere. Economy is perfect — five words.

jokes.text: We're already printing all of our internal memos on the back of my kids' art.
jokes.setup: Jack is pushing for 5% cuts in office supplies
jokes.punchline: Pete reveals they've already pushed cost-cutting so far that children's artwork is their paper supply — delivered with total resignation
jokes.explanation: Solid Pete joke — his defeated middle-management pathos is well-served by the image of his kids' artwork being used as corporate stationery. Specific and visual.

jokes.text: The Harry Potter theme park is a huge hit with both anglophiles and pedophiles.
jokes.setup: Jack is listing Universal Media's profitable divisions to contrast with NBC's failure
jokes.punchline: The list of Harry Potter fans ends with 'and pedophiles' — a dark but structurally perfect addition that subverts the corporate spin
jokes.explanation: The dark-list joke format is well-executed — 'anglophiles and pedophiles' rhymes, which gives it extra punch. The rhyme feels almost accidental which is even funnier. Slightly familiar as a joke type but crisp execution.

jokes.text: The movie division has a James Cameron movie the whole world will see, whether they like it or not.
jokes.setup: Jack is cataloguing Universal Media's profitable assets
jokes.punchline: 'Whether they like it or not' — an honest admission that Avatar-era Cameron films were cultural obligations rather than genuine crowd-pleasers, spoken with corporate pride
jokes.explanation: Sharp cultural observation about James Cameron's cultural dominance circa 2010. The joke is in Jack framing coerced viewership as a selling point — very in-character for his corporate worldview.

jokes.text: Only NBC continues to be the engorged whitehead on the otherwise flawless face of universal media.
jokes.setup: Jack has been cataloguing profitable divisions
jokes.punchline: NBC is described as an 'engorged whitehead' on an otherwise flawless face — a grotesque, specific metaphor that's also accurate corporate self-flagellation
jokes.explanation: 'Engorged whitehead' is an inspired, viscerally specific image for NBC's corporate position — the word 'engorged' doing especially heavy lifting. The juxtaposition of a gross dermatological term with corporate meta-commentary is very 30 Rock. Jack saying this about his own network with resignation is perfect character work.

jokes.text: Lemon, why are you spending so much money on wigs? Tracy's head size keeps changing.
jokes.setup: Jack reviews the budget line items
jokes.punchline: The wig expenditure is explained by Tracy's head literally changing size — a gloriously absurd piece of Tracy lore delivered as a mundane business fact
jokes.explanation: Perfect 30 Rock economy: one throwaway line that implies an entire offscreen world of chaos. Tracy's head changing size is absurd but stated as fact. Liz's matter-of-fact delivery of the explanation is as funny as the content.

jokes.text: Oh, it's just a vanity credit, Lemon. A low-cost way to make someone feel more important. Like executive producer Ashton Kutcher, or secretary of state Hillary Clinton.
jokes.setup: Jack dismisses Jenna's new producer credit as meaningless
jokes.punchline: The examples he gives of 'vanity credits': Ashton Kutcher (plausibly a jab at celebrity producers) and Secretary of State Hillary Clinton — the escalation from showbiz to geopolitics is perfect
jokes.explanation: The list joke works because of the escalation from showbiz (Ashton Kutcher as a celebrity EP is believable as a joke) to the geopolitical (dismissing the Secretary of State as a vanity title). Jack's worldview — that all titles are essentially status games — is crystallized in one line. The specificity of 'Hillary Clinton' rather than a generic politician makes it land harder. Strong quotability.

jokes.text: Am I late for the producers meeting? [Eye contact beat]
jokes.setup: Jack just explained Jenna's new producer credit is a meaningless vanity title
jokes.punchline: Jenna immediately enters asking if she's late for the producers meeting — proving she has taken the vanity credit completely seriously, while Jack and Liz must now hold eye contact with her
jokes.explanation: The timing is impeccable — she walks in at precisely the moment Jack finishes explaining why the credit is meaningless. Her total sincerity about the producer meeting is perfectly Jenna. The running visual of everyone making eye contact adds to the physical comedy.

jokes.text: Eye contact. [Jenna insists; Jack and Liz comply]
jokes.setup: Jenna's contract stipulates mandatory eye contact
jokes.punchline: Jenna enforces the clause immediately; Jack and Liz are contractually obligated to stare at her
jokes.explanation: The visual comedy of Jack Donaghy being forced to maintain intense eye contact with Jenna is worth points on its own. Establishes a running gag for the episode.

jokes.text: First, I need you to go to the dry cleaners for me and find out how martinizing works. I've always been curious.
jokes.setup: Tracy is giving his new page instructions for the day
jokes.punchline: The first task is not something useful but satisfying his personal intellectual curiosity about dry-cleaning chemistry — 'I've always been curious' delivered with complete sincerity
jokes.explanation: Tracy Jordan using a page as a research assistant to answer his personal curiosity about 'martinizing' is beautifully specific absurdism. The earnest 'I've always been curious' is doing a lot of work.

jokes.text: Then I need you to be back by noon to make the bathroom smell like sandalwood before I wreck it.
jokes.setup: Tracy is listing tasks for his page
jokes.punchline: 'Make the bathroom smell like sandalwood before I wreck it' — the casual admission that he will immediately destroy the ambiance he's requesting, delivered as a standard logistical instruction
jokes.explanation: 'Before I wreck it' is a perfect comedy turn — the sensory preparation for an act of immediate destruction. The gap between 'sandalwood' (refined) and 'wreck it' (crude) is the whole joke, and it's completely Tracy.

jokes.text: I'm not Kenneth, sir. My name's Brian. Kenneth got fired at the end of last season.
jokes.setup: Tracy has been giving instructions to his new page as if he's Kenneth
jokes.punchline: The new page reveals he's not Kenneth and directly references the season finale as 'the end of last season' — a meta acknowledgment of the show's own continuity
jokes.explanation: 30 Rock's meta-awareness lands well here. The new page referencing 'last season' as a real temporal marker treats the show's narrative as a transparent fictional construct, which is perfectly in keeping with the show's sensibility.

jokes.text: Of course. I knew that.
jokes.setup: Brian has just told Tracy he's not Kenneth
jokes.punchline: Tracy's completely unconvincing 'Of course. I knew that.' — clearly he had no idea
jokes.explanation: A reliable comic beat — the character pretending they knew something they clearly didn't — but it's familiar and the execution is standard. Functions as a button to the scene.

jokes.text: Did you know that if you're a pilot, that Chili's will seat you right away, even if the pilot's dinner companion has just been yelling at the hostess?
jokes.setup: Liz is asked how things are going with Carol
jokes.punchline: Her answer is a specific anecdote about the perks of dating a pilot — being seated at Chili's immediately — and the parenthetical admission that SHE was the one yelling at the hostess
jokes.explanation: This is excellent Liz Lemon characterization compressed into one sentence: the benefit of dating a pilot (prestige seating) is at Chili's (she's not fancy), and she was just yelling at the hostess (she's difficult). Each element characterizes her precisely. The specific detail of Chili's is crucial — any upscale restaurant would ruin it.

jokes.text: You are the Jackie O of our time.
jokes.setup: Liz has described the Chili's anecdote as a relationship perk
jokes.punchline: Jack's deadpan comparison of Liz to Jackie Kennedy Onassis — one of the most glamorous women in American history — is pure ironic inflation
jokes.explanation: A reliable 30 Rock beat — Jack deploying a grandiose compliment to undercut Liz — but this one is somewhat predictable. Economy is perfect; the joke itself is familiar.

jokes.text: He doesn't stay with you when he's here? Why would he? Those Starwinds are nice! I mean, the bathtubs are so much cleaner than at home.
jokes.setup: Jack is surprised Carol doesn't stay at Liz's apartment
jokes.punchline: Liz enthusiastically endorses Carol staying at the hotel instead — her bathtub is apparently so dirty that a chain hotel is a genuine upgrade
jokes.explanation: A good character beat — Liz's squalid living standards are encoded in her agreeing that a Starwind hotel is nicer than her apartment. The specificity of the bathtub makes it funnier than a general cleanliness joke.

jokes.text: It's almost as bad as 'climax.'
jokes.setup: Liz is discussing her discomfort with relationship language (the word 'relationship' itself)
jokes.punchline: She compares her aversion to 'relationship' to her aversion to 'climax' — a word that functions both as a relationship/intimacy term and in its literal sense
jokes.explanation: A neat wordplay beat — 'climax' as both relationship word and sexual term creates a double layer of Liz's discomfort. Her squeamishness about intimacy language is well-established character comedy.

jokes.text: 'please, Avery, I'm using the commode right now.'
jokes.setup: Jack is explaining the mundane domestic reality that follows vacation — 'one of you says we should redecorate'
jokes.punchline: The example of cohabitation reality is Jack being caught on the commode when Avery wants to discuss redecorating — the specific word 'commode' is doing comic work as a Donaghy-ism
jokes.explanation: The contrast between Jack's highbrow vocabulary ('commode') and the low subject matter is mild character comedy. Not a standout, but characterful.

jokes.text: If I give in, then I'm no longer the Alpha in my house. Before you know it, she'll have me wearing jeans and reading fiction!
jokes.setup: Jack is explaining why he can't simply say yes to Avery's redecorating request
jokes.punchline: The slippery slope Jack fears: loss of alpha status leading to... wearing jeans and reading fiction. These terrify him equally to any genuine loss of power.
jokes.explanation: Outstanding character joke. The escalation from 'loss of alpha status' to 'wearing jeans and reading fiction' is the joke — for Jack Donaghy, these casual middle-class habits represent total civilizational collapse. 'Reading fiction' especially is the perfect pinnacle of what he fears: the frivolous, unproductive, emotionally soft pastime he associates with weakness. Could only be Jack. Deeply quotable.

jokes.text: Meeting someone in a hotel room twice a month is not a relationship... just ask any hooker.
jokes.setup: Liz has said 'you're in no position to judge' — implying her situation with Carol is fine
jokes.punchline: Jack reframes her relationship structure as prostitution — and cites hookers as expert sources on the matter
jokes.explanation: The joke is in Jack treating hookers as legitimate relationship consultants and citing them as reference sources with complete seriousness. Solid but not exceptional.

jokes.text: Oh, stop saying 'relationship'! I'm sorry, I was going to say 'climax.' Aah!
jokes.setup: Jack is pushing Liz to think about her 'relationship' with Carol; Liz reacts with aversion to the word 'relationship'
jokes.punchline: Liz's correction — 'I was going to say climax' — is also aversive to her, creating a callback to her earlier discomfort with that word, and she shrieks at herself
jokes.explanation: Good callback to the earlier 'climax' joke — both words send Liz into panic. The self-directed shriek is a nice physical button.

jokes.text: Oh, I love this. It takes people and turns them into amounts of money.
jokes.setup: Liz shows Jack a line-item budget
jokes.punchline: Jack's delight that people have been reduced to financial figures — delivered with genuine warmth, as if this is the most human thing he's encountered all day
jokes.explanation: Classic Jack Donaghy — his most tender emotion is directed at financial abstraction of human beings. 'Takes people and turns them into amounts of money' is spoken with the warmth others reserve for puppies. Strong character integration.

jokes.text: Except for Tracy, I'm the most person on the show!
jokes.setup: Jenna is reviewing the budget and discovering her value relative to others
jokes.punchline: 'I'm the most person on the show' — grammatically broken but emotionally revealing; Jenna has compared herself to a line item and won (sort of)
jokes.explanation: The grammatical collapse of 'most person' is the joke — Jenna is so narcissistically oriented toward comparisons that she breaks language trying to rank herself. The qualifier 'except for Tracy' shows a vestige of self-awareness.

jokes.text: You should fire grace from wardrobe. She doesn't do anything. Fire grace? Come on, you'd have to be a heartless monster... I'll do it.
jokes.setup: Jenna suggests firing Grace; Liz starts to object morally
jokes.punchline: Liz cuts herself off mid-moral-objection to immediately volunteer to fire Grace — the speed of her reversal is the joke
jokes.explanation: The structure is clean — set up the moral objection ('you'd have to be a heartless monster'), subvert it immediately ('I'll do it'). The speed is everything; it works because Liz is often self-righteous but can also be ruthlessly practical.

jokes.text: Your health insurance will remain in effect until the end of this sentence.
jokes.setup: Liz is firing Grace, a long-time employee who has been at TGS since the Jack Paar show
jokes.punchline: The health insurance — typically a meaningful severance benefit — lasts only for the duration of the sentence in which she announces it, which she is now ending
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's best jokes and arguably one of the best jokes in 30 Rock's run. The self-referential structure (the sentence IS the insurance period) is formally brilliant — a meta joke about language that also lands as pure dark comedy about corporate cruelty. 'Until the end of this sentence' has a perfect arc: you hear 'sentence,' expect 'a year' or 'six months,' and then realize as she finishes speaking that the sentence is now ending. Maximum funny per word. Quotable, rewatch-worthy, and genuinely clever.

jokes.text: What a shank job.
jokes.setup: Grace has just been fired after decades at TGS
jokes.punchline: Her only response to such brutal treatment is the casual, resigned 'What a shank job.' — the understatement of a woman who has seen everything
jokes.explanation: Grace's weary profanity-adjacent response to her firing — 'shank job' feels like old-school industry slang — is a great button. The delivery of total non-drama from someone who should be devastated is tragicomic.

jokes.text: Kenneth, I knew you'd come back! Let me smell your head.
jokes.setup: Tracy sees a new woman and hallucinates her as Kenneth
jokes.punchline: Tracy's greeting to 'Kenneth' is to immediately ask to smell his head — this is apparently a normal greeting in their relationship
jokes.explanation: Tracy wanting to smell Kenneth's head as a form of greeting/identification is the right level of Tracy-specific absurdism. The warmth of the reunion makes the weirdness funnier.

jokes.text: This is a woman's blazer from a very expensive blazer shop called Rico's.
jokes.setup: Tracy wants to smell 'Kenneth's' head to confirm his identity
jokes.punchline: The person he's mistaking for Kenneth identifies herself and her blazer's provenance, as if this corrects anything
jokes.explanation: A functional beat — the joke is that identifying the blazer as from Rico's is irrelevant information in this context. Not especially sharp but serves the scene.

jokes.text: I'm sorry, but my heart is playing tricks on my eyes. Just like my kidneys did to my lungs that time.
jokes.setup: Tracy apologizes for the hallucination
jokes.punchline: The apology is followed by a reference to his organs playing tricks on each other as if this is a documented medical history — 'that time' implies a specific prior incident
jokes.explanation: The extension of 'heart playing tricks on eyes' to 'kidneys doing to lungs what my heart did to my eyes' is absurdist body-horror comedy. 'That time' implies there was a specific documented incident of inter-organ deception. Deeply Tracy. The internal logic of his medical history is the joke.

jokes.text: Am I going crazy again? Should I get my rainbow wig out of storage?
jokes.setup: Tracy is worried about hallucinating Kenneth
jokes.punchline: His proposed solution to going crazy is to retrieve a rainbow wig from storage — implying this is an established crazy-person protocol for him
jokes.explanation: Tracy's 'crazy again' protocol apparently involves a rainbow wig in storage — an absurd but specific detail that implies a rich backstory of Tracy's mental health management. 'Again' is doing heavy work.

jokes.text: Like the world cup. I'll try.
jokes.setup: Liz tells Tracy to tell himself 'this is not real, I am in control of this' when he hallucinates
jokes.punchline: Tracy relates 'I am in control of this' to the World Cup — the connection is completely opaque and unexplained, which is the joke
jokes.explanation: Pure Tracy absurdism — the World Cup as his reference point for maintaining control of reality is inexplicable and therefore funny. The joke relies entirely on the non-sequitur; there's no actual logical connection, which is the point.

jokes.text: Would you rather have to start every sentence you say for the rest of your life with Urkel's catchphrase, 'Did I do that?' Or be Siamese twins with Sharon Stone for a year?
jokes.setup: Liz walks in on writers apparently playing 'Would You Rather'
jokes.punchline: The two options are hilariously specific and degrading: the Urkel option makes you a buffoon forever; the Siamese twin option pairs you with Sharon Stone specifically for a year
jokes.explanation: The 'Would You Rather' game establishes both a running gag and Liz's participation — her immediate answer ('Did I do that?') reveals she's not even pretending to deliberate, she just answered in character. The specificity of Sharon Stone (not a generic celebrity) shows real joke-writing craft.

jokes.text: Did I do that? Carol!
jokes.setup: Liz has been asked the 'Would You Rather' — Urkel or Sharon Stone
jokes.punchline: Liz answers immediately with 'Did I do that?' (Urkel catchphrase — she chose the Urkel option) and then without a beat calls 'Carol!' because her phone rang
jokes.explanation: The Urkel catchphrase as Liz's immediate phone greeting is the accidental joke — she answered the hypothetical and then immediately used the catchphrase contextually appropriately. Nice structure.

jokes.text: Try five miles high. And no, I have not.
jokes.setup: Liz asks if Carol has joined the Mile High Club
jokes.punchline: Carol claims to have gone five miles high (as a commercial pilot, higher altitude), then answers the actual question ('no, I have not') — the boast and the honesty are simultaneous
jokes.explanation: The misdirection is clever: 'try five miles high' makes you expect a brag, but 'and no, I have not' deflates it — he's both more elite and more celibate than the question implies. Crisp.

jokes.text: No, but once, when I was in the air force, I saw Mr. T in a Pizza Hut.
jokes.setup: Liz asks if Carol ever saw a UFO up there
jokes.punchline: Instead of a UFO story, Carol has a completely earthbound celebrity sighting at a Pizza Hut — stated with equal gravitas as if it's comparable
jokes.explanation: Perfect anti-climax: asked about UFOs (the most extraordinary thing imaginable), Carol responds with a perfectly mundane celebrity sighting, in a Pizza Hut of all places. Mr. T specifically — not a glamorous celebrity — and Pizza Hut — not a glamorous restaurant — makes this maximally specific. The gravitas with which he delivers it is the key.

jokes.text: Was the air force like Top Gun? Yeah, but with a lot more volleyball.
jokes.setup: Liz asks if the air force was like Top Gun
jokes.punchline: Carol confirms it was exactly like Top Gun — but specifically the homoerotic volleyball scene, implying that's the most accurate element of the film
jokes.explanation: The joke plays on the cultural shorthand of Top Gun's famous volleyball scene — confirming Air Force culture via the film's most famous/mocked element. Economical and lands well.

jokes.text: You ever kill anyone? Sucked a mechanic into my engine once.
jokes.setup: Liz is rapid-firing getting-to-know-you questions at Carol
jokes.punchline: Carol's answer to 'you ever kill anyone' is a casual, specific, non-military death — a mechanic sucked into an engine — delivered with total matter-of-factness
jokes.explanation: The setup ('ever kill anyone?') invites a heroic military story; the punchline is an accidental, industrial death described as casually as a fender-bender. 'Once' does enormous work — implying it happened, it was noted, and he moved on. The specificity of 'mechanic into my engine' rather than something vague makes it darkly hilarious. High quotability.

jokes.text: Are you on Facebook?
jokes.setup: Carol has just casually admitted to killing someone
jokes.punchline: Liz's immediate follow-up question — 'Are you on Facebook?' — treats the death admission as a conversational speed bump before moving to the next getting-to-know-you question
jokes.explanation: The perfect button to the mechanic death: Liz doesn't react at all to the killing, she just moves on to her next question. 'Facebook?' as the follow-up to manslaughter is the joke — the bathos of social media next to accidental death. Pure Liz. The silence/non-reaction is as important as the line.

jokes.text: Ooh. [flowers left by passenger in first-class lavatory]
jokes.setup: Carol gives Liz flowers as a gift
jokes.punchline: He explains they were left in the first-class lavatory — the romantic gesture is made with used, abandoned bathroom flowers
jokes.explanation: A gentle gross-out: the romantic gift is discarded bathroom flowers. The 'ooh' before the revelation sets up the disappointment. Mild but effective.

jokes.text: Uh... uh, yeah. Of course. I'll just have to run home first and take some plates out of the bathroom.
jokes.setup: Carol asks if it'd be okay to stay at Liz's place for the weekend
jokes.punchline: Liz agrees but mentions she needs to first remove plates from her bathroom — implying she keeps dishes in the bathroom, for reasons unspecified
jokes.explanation: Perfectly Liz Lemon. The joke implies she eats in the bathroom regularly enough to have established a plate situation there — and that this is the obstacle to having a guest. The parenthetical delivery ('I'll just have to run home first and take some plates out of the bathroom') as if it's a normal errand is the masterpiece of understatement. Very quotable.

jokes.text: I just can't believe that every Starwind suite in the city is taken. Me neither. The lady said they're all booked up for something called Jackfest.
jokes.setup: Carol is frustrated he can't get a Starwind room
jokes.punchline: All rooms are booked for 'Jackfest' — which Liz clearly knows is Jack's doing, even if she acts confused
jokes.explanation: The gag of Jack booking every Starwind room under 'Jackfest' is charming — the name is characteristically grandiose. Setup for the Jack reveal.

jokes.text: How many rooms did you book? It's for your own good, Lemon.
jokes.setup: Liz confronts Jack about Jackfest
jokes.punchline: Jack immediately confirms he did it — and justifies it as altruism. He doesn't deny or apologize.
jokes.explanation: Jack's paternalistic meddling is well-established character comedy. The joke is in his complete lack of shame — 'it's for your own good' is delivered as if buying out a hotel chain for someone's benefit is normal.

jokes.text: A middle-aged woman saying 'dude stuff'... is that on my sadness scavenger hunt? Why, yes, it is.
jokes.setup: Liz says she doesn't like her 'life stuff mixing with her dude stuff'
jokes.punchline: Jack has a 'sadness scavenger hunt' — a list of pathetic Liz behaviors he collects — and Liz saying 'dude stuff' has completed an item on it
jokes.explanation: The concept of a 'sadness scavenger hunt' — where Jack tracks Liz's pathetic behaviors as an ongoing catalog — is inspired. It condenses their entire relationship dynamic into a conceit: Jack as bemused anthropologist of Liz's self-sabotage. The self-answering 'Why, yes, it is' is a perfect deadpan button. Original concept, strong character integration.

jokes.text: I'm like that woman on the Food Network whose husband only comes home on the weekends, and she spends the rest of her time eating and drinking with her gay friends.
jokes.setup: Liz is defending her 'separate but intersecting lifestyles' arrangement with Carol
jokes.punchline: The person she's modeling her ideal relationship on is the Barefoot Contessa — a specific, slightly sad aspiration for a romantic ideal
jokes.explanation: Liz's romantic ideal being a Food Network personality whose husband is absent and whose social life revolves around gay friends is an excellent self-indictment. The description is specific enough to be funny even without knowing who the Barefoot Contessa is.

jokes.text: Her name is the Barefoot Contessa, Lemon, and you will never be like her, starting with the barefoot part.
jokes.setup: Liz compares herself to the Barefoot Contessa
jokes.punchline: Jack points out the many ways Liz falls short of this idol, leading with the most physical/superficial — she can't even be barefoot like Ina Garten
jokes.explanation: 'Starting with the barefoot part' is a lovely comic diminishment — Jack begins the list of Liz's deficiencies with the most basic physical requirement (being barefoot) and implies the list continues. The 'starting with' structure implies the problems go much deeper.

jokes.text: I'll have you know that I wore sandals this summer, over socks... In a dream.
jokes.setup: Jack says Liz can't even approximate the Barefoot Contessa lifestyle
jokes.punchline: Liz's defense escalates in defeat: sandals (not barefoot), then over socks (not even close), then 'in a dream' (didn't happen at all)
jokes.explanation: A three-stage escalating collapse: sandals (acceptable compromise) → over socks (defeats the purpose entirely) → in a dream (none of this happened). Each beat is funnier than the last, and the structure of building toward 'in a dream' is impeccable — she started defending herself and ended by admitting she's never even managed this in sleep. Pure Liz Lemon character comedy at its finest. Highly quotable.

jokes.text: Welcome to the Late Show with David Letterman. Please have your tickets out. And now, as with all studio audiences, we will sort you according to attractiveness. Front, front, back, balcony...
jokes.setup: Tracy encounters a studio audience (presumably for TGS or nearby) and hallucinates or imagines himself as a Letterman-style host
jokes.punchline: Tracy announces they will sort the audience by attractiveness and begins doing so — 'front, front, back, balcony' — as if this is standard protocol
jokes.explanation: Tracy sorting an audience by attractiveness is a great absurdist moment. The specific cadence of 'front, front, back, balcony' implies he's mid-process and making rapid judgments. Very Tracy.

jokes.text: No, you do not exist! I'm in control of this!
jokes.setup: Tracy suddenly sees someone he thinks might be Kenneth hallucination during the Letterman bit
jokes.punchline: He breaks from the audience-sorting to directly address the hallucination using Liz's prescribed mantra — 'I'm in control of this!' — while still mid-fake-Letterman-show
jokes.explanation: The callback to Liz's anti-hallucination mantra is functional — Tracy deploying 'I'm in control of this' while clearly not in control. Doesn't add much beyond confirming he heard the advice.

jokes.text: First thing you need is tequila... Stop. Wait. No. The Barefoot Contessa... I love this show.
jokes.setup: Carol starts to suggest something for their evening, starting with 'first thing you need is tequila'
jokes.punchline: Liz interrupts — it's the Barefoot Contessa on TV. The domestic TV discovery overrides Carol's romantic suggestion; both are equally excited about Ina Garten
jokes.explanation: The callback to the Barefoot Contessa pays off here as the actual show appears on TV, and both Carol and Liz share genuine enthusiasm for it. Sets up the relationship compatibility jokes that follow.

jokes.text: This is one of the three things in the world I like... Ina Garten, sweater weather, and... When Muppets present at award shows? Wow, yes! Me too.
jokes.setup: Carol and Liz are discovering shared interests
jokes.punchline: Carol's three favorite things list: Ina Garten (food TV), sweater weather (mild meteorological comfort), and when Muppets present at award shows — and Liz completes the third item before he can say it
jokes.explanation: The list's escalation is charming: Ina Garten → sweater weather → Muppets presenting at award shows. The third item is surprisingly specific and niche, and Liz completing Carol's sentence before he says it confirms their connection. The whole joke establishes that their compatibility is real, but also very specific and slightly goofy.

jokes.text: I've never met anyone before who had the exact same idea as me about what to do with Palestine. It would work, right? Of course it would work.
jokes.setup: Carol and Liz are marveling at how much they agree on everything
jokes.punchline: Among their points of agreement: a specific geopolitical solution for Palestine — both speak of it with total confidence but never specify what it is
jokes.explanation: The joke is the gap between the specificity of agreement ('the exact same idea') and the complete absence of any detail about what the idea is. The mutual reassurance ('it would work, right? Of course it would work') mimics how people validate each other's confidences without scrutiny. Their shared ignorance as shared intimacy is a sharp observational point.

jokes.text: No, no, I can't... I can't live like this anymore. I'm not like Jeffrey Garten. I'm not as strong as that guy!
jokes.setup: Liz and Carol have been watching the Barefoot Contessa and bonding over shared preferences; Liz suggests they're perfect like Jeffrey and Ina
jokes.punchline: Carol has a breakdown about not being able to emotionally sustain the Barefoot Contessa lifestyle — specifically, he cannot handle being Jeffrey Garten (Ina's absent husband)
jokes.explanation: Carol's breakdown being specifically about his inability to be Jeffrey Garten is absurd and beautifully unexpected. 'I'm not as strong as that guy' — treating the Barefoot Contessa's absent husband as a figure of remarkable emotional fortitude — is a perfect twist. The whole structure of having a relationship crisis about a cooking show host is very 30 Rock.

jokes.text: I can't go from woman to woman to woman anymore... How many women have you been with? I'd rather not say. It's shameful. I mean, I'm a pit. Six. Oh, that's not so great.
jokes.setup: Carol is building up to an emotional confession about his romantic past, implying a vast number of women
jokes.punchline: The shameful number is six. Liz's 'Oh, that's not so great' is the deflation — six is not impressive for a 'I've been with so many women' speech
jokes.explanation: Perfect misdirection — the dramatic buildup ('I'd rather not say, it's shameful, I'm a pit') sets up a large, embarrassing number. Six is the perfect anti-climax: too few to be impressive, not enough to actually justify the shame speech. Liz's flat 'Oh, that's not so great' lands the killing blow.

jokes.text: Carol had a complete meltdown about the state of our relationship. I can't believe I tried to clean my bathtub for this.
jokes.setup: Liz is updating Jack on the Carol situation
jokes.punchline: Liz's emotional response to the meltdown focuses entirely on the wasted bathtub-cleaning effort — the inconvenience of a chore, not the emotional content of the relationship crisis
jokes.explanation: The bathtub cleaning as Liz's primary grievance about the relationship crisis is perfectly Lemon — she cleaned her notoriously dirty tub for this emotional inconvenience. The callback to the dirty bathtub established earlier makes this land harder.

jokes.text: I finally got him to sleep. I had to spoon him for, like, an hour. And I was the outer spoon.
jokes.setup: Liz explains how she got Carol to calm down
jokes.punchline: 'And I was the outer spoon' — the gender-role subversion of Liz as big spoon to a weeping pilot is the punchline, stated matter-of-factly
jokes.explanation: Liz as the outer spoon to Carol is a great inversion — it completes the picture of Carol's breakdown perfectly and is stated as a resigned logistical fact rather than a complaint. The specificity of 'outer spoon' rather than just 'big spoon' is a nice choice.

jokes.text: And now she's sleeping peacefully while Fabius has retreated to his den, where he is drinking scotch and playing Snood.
jokes.setup: Jack is explaining his Fabian strategy victory for the day
jokes.punchline: The grand Roman general persona ('Fabius has retreated to his den') dissolves into the reality: he's drinking scotch and playing Snood (an early 2000s casual computer game)
jokes.explanation: The Fabian strategy conceit collides with the absurd specificity of 'playing Snood' — the gap between Roman general rhetoric and a circa-2002 browser game is the joke. 'Fabius has retreated to his den' sets up genuine grandeur and then 'playing Snood' demolishes it. The choice of Snood (not chess, not something impressive) is the key — it's perfectly chosen for maximum deflation.

jokes.text: When Avery got home from work, I noticed that she had some paint samples in her purse, so I immediately asked her if her sister had done anything crazy lately, and guess what...She had. Avery talked about that for about an hour, her anger eventually transforming into some rather interesting sex.
jokes.setup: Jack describes successfully deploying the Fabian strategy
jokes.punchline: The maneuvering works — the distraction of the sister's drama converts to 'rather interesting sex'
jokes.explanation: 'Her anger eventually transforming into some rather interesting sex' is a good phrase — the euphemism 'interesting' does a lot of work. The whole sequence shows Jack's manipulation is clinical and effective, which is both funny and slightly disturbing.

jokes.text: Just sending her a link to this cool site... funkyvintagewallpaper.com. Lemon, don't! She keeps her BlackBerry in bed with her. And send. Damn it, Lemon! It has to be elk tongue!
jokes.setup: Jack has successfully avoided the wallpaper debate for another day via Fabian retreat
jokes.punchline: Liz sabotages him in real time by sending Avery a wallpaper website link — Jack panics ('she keeps her BlackBerry in bed with her'), Liz sends it anyway, and Jack's Fabian composure collapses into 'It has to be elk tongue!'
jokes.explanation: Jack's strategic composure crumbling in real time as Liz trolls him is great — the payoff is Jack shrieking about 'elk tongue' (his color preference from 10 minutes earlier), finally abandoning all Fabian dignity. 'It has to be elk tongue!' is the most unguarded Jack has been all episode.

jokes.text: Yesterday, I went to the gym. And this morning, I made love to my wife. And she was still asleep, so I didn't have to be gentle.
jokes.setup: Pete is explaining the benefits of Jenna's producer promotion — he now has free time
jokes.punchline: The escalation of Pete's freedom: gym, then sex with his sleeping wife, then 'so I didn't have to be gentle' — the third beat is a dark revelation about his marriage
jokes.explanation: The escalation here is near-perfect. 'Went to the gym' (healthy), 'made love to my wife' (connubial), 'she was still asleep' (concerning), 'didn't have to be gentle' (disturbing). Each step is fine until the last beat which recontextualizes everything as deeply dysfunctional. Pete's total lack of self-awareness about the wrongness of this is key. Shocking, dark, and perfectly structured. High quotability despite (because of) its darkness.

jokes.text: That's one of the most upsetting things I have ever imagined. Are you sure? Think about it again. Yes.
jokes.setup: Pete has just described making love to his sleeping wife without being gentle
jokes.punchline: Liz says it's the most upsetting thing she's ever imagined; Pete asks her to reconsider; she does ('yes')
jokes.explanation: The button to Pete's horror: Liz's revulsion, Pete's inexplicable confidence that thinking about it more will improve it, and Liz confirming it doesn't. Pete's 'are you sure? Think about it again' is almost childlike in its obliviousness.

jokes.text: Liz, the writers can't take a car service at night anymore. I've crunched the numbers, and it's cheaper for us to just replace anyone who gets murdered.
jokes.setup: Budget cuts are being implemented; Pete delivers news about writer transportation
jokes.punchline: The cost-benefit analysis concludes that replacing murdered writers is cheaper than safe transport — stated with the tone of a routine memo
jokes.explanation: Excellent dark corporate comedy. The joke treats human life as a balance sheet item — 'cheaper to replace anyone who gets murdered' is the logical endpoint of the cost-cutting premise. The deadpan delivery of something monstrous as a routine business decision is the 30 Rock specialty. Economy is near-perfect — maximum horror per word. Very quotable.

jokes.text: Every new pattern Avery showed me, I would simply say, 'yes, I like that one too.' And she was so overwhelmed with the choices that she made a mistake. She suggested that we consult her old college friend, who's an interior designer. His name is James. Not Jim, not Jimmy... Jamessss.
jokes.setup: Jack is explaining how his Fabian strategy worked — he agreed with all of Avery's choices until she made a strategic error
jokes.punchline: The mistake was suggesting her interior designer friend 'James' — and Jack's elongated 'Jamessss' signals he's already detected and plans to exploit this man's gayness
jokes.explanation: The elongated 'Jamessss' is a great bit of comic shorthand — Jack's intonation tells you everything about what he's planning. The setup is efficient and the promise of the James plot is intriguing.

jokes.text: Do you know what a prize I am in the gay community? There's a term for it. I'm a bear... And I'm a daddy bear.
jokes.setup: Jack is explaining his plan to charm interior designer James by leveraging his gay community value
jokes.punchline: Jack identifies himself using gay subculture terminology — 'bear' and 'daddy bear' — with complete confidence and no irony
jokes.explanation: Jack's confident knowledge of his own gay community status (bear, then specifically daddy bear) is perfect character comedy — he's approached this strategically, done the research, and arrived at a confident conclusion. The pause between 'I'm a bear' and 'And I'm a daddy bear' (with an implied correction/upgrade) is excellent comic timing.

jokes.text: Have you seen my eyes, Lemon? Yep. They're very blue. Like a Mykonos sky. Mark Foley once called them 'piercing.'
jokes.setup: Jack is assessing his appeal to James, the gay interior designer
jokes.punchline: His list of eye credentials includes Mark Foley calling them 'piercing' — Foley being the Republican congressman who resigned over inappropriate messages to male Congressional pages
jokes.explanation: The Mark Foley reference is brilliantly specific. Foley's political scandal (soliciting underage Congressional pages) makes him the worst possible character reference for Jack's appeal to gay men — both politically and morally. Jack treats it as a credential, which is even funnier. Very 30 Rock in its political specificity.

jokes.text: Just one hour of flirty chatting with James, and you know what I'll get. Not a Glaad award, I know that.
jokes.setup: Jack is projecting confidence about charming James
jokes.punchline: Liz's dry 'Not a GLAAD award, I know that' — acknowledging that whatever Jack plans to do with James is not gay-friendly
jokes.explanation: Liz's GLAAD award line is a tight ironic observation — correctly identifying that Jack's plan to manipulate a gay man for wallpaper advantage is not exemplary LGBTQ allyship. Economical.

jokes.text: Elk tongue.
jokes.setup: Jack has just said he'll get what he wants from James
jokes.punchline: One word: 'Elk tongue.' — stated with quiet certainty as the entire justification for his manipulation
jokes.explanation: Perfect economy — two words summarize Jack's entire motivation. 'Elk tongue' as the punchline to a conversation about geopolitics, manipulation, and gay community dynamics is the essence of 30 Rock's bathos. The understatement is total.

jokes.text: Would you rather let go of your precious autonomy, and let Carol into your life? Or would you rather teach your cat to dial 911?
jokes.setup: Jack is laying out Liz's choices about her relationship with Carol
jokes.punchline: Option two: teach her cat to dial 911 — implying a future of medical emergencies without human support, reduced to a cat as emergency contact
jokes.explanation: The binary choice is excellent: the first option is reasonable (let someone in), the second is a darkly specific projection of Liz's lonely future (relying on a pet for emergency medical assistance). 'Teach your cat to dial 911' is specific enough to be funny and bleak enough to land as a real threat.

jokes.text: First of all, I'm tired of playing 'would you rather.' And second of all, you know that I have Life Alert.
jokes.setup: Jack presents a 'would you rather' framing for Liz's life choices
jokes.punchline: Liz's rebuttal references her Life Alert — she's already prepared for medical emergencies alone, at an age where Life Alert is not typically needed
jokes.explanation: Liz having Life Alert — the elderly emergency device — is a perfect Liz Lemon detail. She's already conceded the point about being alone but solved the emergency problem with technology. The callback to the writers' 'would you rather' game is also a nice touch.

jokes.text: Oh, I pushed it. I need a phone.
jokes.setup: Liz has mentioned her Life Alert
jokes.punchline: She has accidentally activated her Life Alert and needs a phone, presumably to cancel the emergency call
jokes.explanation: The immediate activation of the Life Alert is a solid physical comedy button. The joke is that she's exactly as helpless as Jack predicted, just seconds after insisting she isn't.

jokes.text: Mr. Jordan, please stop. You're not real. If I threw you in front of a car, it would drive right through you!
jokes.setup: Tracy encounters what he believes is another Kenneth hallucination
jokes.punchline: Tracy threatens to throw his page in front of a car to test whether he's real — the logic being that cars pass through hallucinations
jokes.explanation: Tracy's hallucination-testing methodology — throwing someone in front of traffic — is absurd but internally logical. The terrifying calmness of the proposed test is the joke.

jokes.text: Would an imaginary me know that you have a mole on your list of pets to get? Or that your favorite color is rainbow?
jokes.setup: Brian is trying to prove to Tracy he's real
jokes.punchline: Brian's evidence: he knows Tracy has a mole on his 'list of pets to get' and that Tracy's favorite color is rainbow — both are delightfully Tracy-specific details
jokes.explanation: Both details are perfect Tracy lore: a mole on his 'list of pets to get' (he has a list; a mole is on it) and favorite color is rainbow (not a real color, and also calls back to the rainbow wig). The specificity of the details proves the page's intimate knowledge — and both details are absurd in Tracy-specific ways.

jokes.text: Of course it would. It would know anything I knew because it sprung from my imagination. [Tracy throws Brian in front of a car anyway]
jokes.setup: Brian argues that an imaginary him wouldn't know these details
jokes.punchline: Tracy logically refutes the argument (a hallucination would know everything he knows since it comes from his mind) — and then apparently throws Brian in front of a car anyway
jokes.explanation: Tracy's counter-argument is actually logically sound — which makes it even funnier. The joke is that he reasons his way to 'the argument doesn't work' and then throws Brian in front of a car anyway. The physical consequence of 'Oh my God! Oh no, I missed it! Do it again!' confirms Brian survived but that Tracy's response to the proof-of-real is excitement at the near miss rather than relief. Brilliant.

jokes.text: Oh, my God! Oh, no, I missed it! Do it again!
jokes.setup: A car narrowly misses Brian after Tracy pushes him
jokes.punchline: Tracy's reaction to the near-miss is disappointment that he missed the spectacle and a request to 'do it again' — as if it were a street performance
jokes.explanation: The perfect button to the car-throwing sequence. 'I missed it! Do it again!' treats nearly killing someone as a disappointing magic trick. Tracy's complete absence of concern for Brian's safety and his focus on the spectacle value is a masterpiece of character-specific absurdism. One of the best Tracy moments in the episode.

jokes.text: Why don't you come back home to TGS and pick the peas out of my fried rice? And the rice. I just want carrots.
jokes.setup: Tracy is pleading with Kenneth to come back
jokes.punchline: Tracy's enticement to return is picking peas out of his fried rice — then 'and the rice,' meaning he just wants carrot delivery service
jokes.explanation: The escalation of Tracy's carrot-only fried rice request (removing peas → removing rice → all he wants is carrots) is an absurdly specific domestic intimacy that characterizes their relationship perfectly. The 'and the rice' afterthought is the kicker.

jokes.text: But I'm real happy here at CBS. They gave me a tote bag with The Mentalist on it!
jokes.setup: Kenneth is explaining why he can't come back to NBC/TGS
jokes.punchline: The reason Kenneth is happy at CBS: a tote bag featuring The Mentalist — the lowness of this perk contrasted with the earnestness of his delight is the joke
jokes.explanation: Kenneth's genuine happiness at a network tote bag (especially one featuring The Mentalist, a show known for being middlebrow rather than prestige) is a beautiful character beat. The specificity of the show on the bag is crucial — it's not HBO or AMC, it's The Mentalist.

jokes.text: Obviously, I'm going to need the tote bag.
jokes.setup: Kenneth has shown Tracy his CBS Mentalist tote bag as evidence of his happiness
jokes.punchline: Tracy's goodbye: he claims the tote bag. This is Tracy's primary concern — not Kenneth's wellbeing or return, but the bag
jokes.explanation: The 'obviously' does enormous work — Tracy treating the tote bag as an obvious entitlement in an emotional farewell scene is perfectly selfish and absurd. The single-word 'obviously' conveys absolute confidence that this is a reasonable position.

jokes.text: I was looking it over, and I've realized something. There's one too many producers, Pete. Okay, I get it. But please... I have five kids. That I don't want to be at home with. No, Pete, it's me.
jokes.setup: Liz has found a budget solution — one producer too many. Pete assumes he's being fired.
jokes.punchline: Pete's plea includes 'I have five kids that I don't want to be at home with' — he's begging not to be fired so he can avoid his own family. Then Liz reveals it's not Pete but herself.
jokes.explanation: Two jokes in one exchange: Pete's admission that he's begging to keep his job primarily to avoid his family is a Pete-defining moment of dark honesty. Then the misdirection pay off — we thought Liz was firing Pete, but she's firing herself. Both beats earn their place.

jokes.text: Hmm, the last time I said that, I was in a three-way with two of the Backstreet Boys.
jokes.setup: Liz says 'I'm not really necessary' about her own position
jokes.punchline: Jenna says the last time she said 'I'm not really necessary' she was in a sexual situation with Backstreet Boys — a non-sequitur that reveals her chaotic personal life
jokes.explanation: Jenna deploying a Backstreet Boys threesome as a contextual reference is perfectly Jenna — her glamorous self-mythology always involves C-list celebrities and sexual adventures. 'Two of the Backstreet Boys' (not all of them, not one, two) is a funny specificity.

jokes.text: But it's because I'm a genius producer I know that you have to fire me. Take my producing fee and amortize it to cover the gaps in transport and electric.
jokes.setup: Jenna is being surprisingly selfless about giving up her producer fee
jokes.punchline: Jenna uses actual production terminology correctly ('amortize,' 'transport and electric') — the joke being that she has genuinely learned producing despite it being a vanity credit
jokes.explanation: The joke is the gap between Jenna being treated as a vanity producer and her actually knowing production terminology. Subverts the earlier dismissal of her credit, but the comedic impact is moderate.

jokes.text: Would you rather be with the person you love forever, but you always have to wear a shirt made out of their pubes, or be alone for the rest of your life, but you get to wear whatever you want? Shirt of pubes.
jokes.setup: The writers resume 'Would You Rather' as Liz arrives
jokes.punchline: Liz answers 'shirt of pubes' without hesitation — she chooses love + discomfort over freedom + loneliness, but the speed and matter-of-factness of the answer is the joke
jokes.explanation: The 'would you rather' game has been a running thread, and this one has the most thematic resonance: Liz's answer (pube shirt) lands as both absurd and emotionally revealing — she would literally wear a shirt of pubes to be with someone she loves. The speed of her answer ('shirt of pubes') undercuts any sentimentality. Structurally, it sets up Carol's return and her emotional arc. Running gag paid off beautifully.

jokes.text: I mean, I had to kick an obese teen off the flight to get a seat, but I really wanted to talk to you.
jokes.setup: Carol has come back after leaving, having apparently gotten a last-minute flight
jokes.punchline: He got the seat by bumping an obese teen — stated as a minor inconvenience he had to handle to get back to Liz
jokes.explanation: The specificity of 'obese teen' (not just any passenger) makes this darker and funnier than a generic bump. Carol's framing — 'I had to' — treats displacing a heavy teenager as a romantic sacrifice.

jokes.text: That's actually not even part of my personality. That's just something that happens to people who change altitude more than four times a day.
jokes.setup: Carol says he's not sorry Liz saw him cry — he's an emotional guy
jokes.punchline: He immediately reverses: his emotionality is not personality but a physiological side effect of changing altitude more than four times daily
jokes.explanation: The medical disclaimer for his breakdown — altitude changes cause emotional volatility more than four times per day — is a great face-saving rationalization that also implies his whole life is a series of altitude-induced emotional episodes.

jokes.text: Is that also why you got so mad watching the Giants game? No, that was because why does Geico have three different spokespeople?
jokes.setup: Liz asks if altitude-induced emotion explains his Giants game anger
jokes.punchline: No — the Giants anger was genuinely about Geico having too many spokespeople. He then lists them: caveman, lizard, stack of money with eyeballs, and the fake Rod Serling.
jokes.explanation: The Geico complaint is a sharp bit of 2010 observational comedy — the company genuinely did have an absurd number of campaigns running simultaneously, and Carol's anger about it while watching a sports game is very true to life. 'Fake Rod Serling' as the fourth spokesperson Liz adds is a nice bonus.

jokes.text: And the fake Rod Serling guy. Oh, my God, right. Thank you.
jokes.setup: Carol has listed three Geico spokespeople
jokes.punchline: Liz adds the fourth one ('fake Rod Serling'), and Carol's 'Oh, my God, right. Thank you.' is a moment of genuine couple-bonding over a shared media grievance
jokes.explanation: A gentler continuation of the Geico joke — the joke here is that this shared grievance is the actual romantic chemistry between them. 'Thank you' as if she's validated his deepest concern is sweet and funny.

jokes.text: I mean, you see how good we are together? Look, Liz, I want this.
jokes.setup: Carol uses the Geico agreement as evidence of their compatibility
jokes.punchline: The romantic declaration follows from a shared complaint about insurance advertising — Carol treats this as meaningful evidence they belong together
jokes.explanation: The joke is in the romantic leap from Geico complaints to 'I want this.' It's a funny non-sequitur transition but not one of the episode's strongest moments.

jokes.text: Two minutes to air. Cast, please set yourselves. Look, you have to get back to the airport, I have a show. How do we move this forward in the time allotted?
jokes.setup: Liz and Carol are in the middle of an emotional relationship conversation
jokes.punchline: The show PA calls two minutes to air; Liz immediately pivots to 'how do we move this forward in the time allotted?' — treating the emotional conversation as a schedule item to be efficiently resolved
jokes.explanation: Liz's project-management approach to emotional conversations is well-established character comedy. 'In the time allotted' applies production scheduling language to intimacy.

jokes.text: All right, let's each say one thing about ourselves that the other person doesn't know on the count of three. Ready? One, two, three. I'm on a waiting list to adopt a kid. Touched by a priest... it's fine. Wait, what?
jokes.setup: They decide to move the relationship forward by sharing something the other doesn't know
jokes.punchline: Carol shares adoption waitlist (sweet). Liz shares 'touched by a priest... it's fine.' — the casual ellipsis and 'it's fine' are doing enormous dark work; Carol's 'wait, what?' confirms this landed wrong
jokes.explanation: Near-perfect joke. The structure is impeccable: simultaneous reveal, one innocent (adoption waitlist), one devastating (priest abuse). '...it's fine' is the greatest two words in the joke — the ellipsis implying she went somewhere dark before correcting herself to 'fine.' Carol's 'wait, what?' is the perfect button. The structural parallel of exchanging secrets makes the contrast maximally effective. Highly quotable, uncomfortable, and brilliant. Among the episode's best.

jokes.text: I never thought you'd make it this far, Lemon. I know, season five... We were supposed to get cancelled. Not just the show, I mean you.
jokes.setup: Jack says he never thought Liz would make it this far
jokes.punchline: Liz assumes he means the show; Jack clarifies he means Liz as a person — she was not expected to survive to this point
jokes.explanation: The meta-referential/in-show double meaning works well: season five as both show milestone and Liz's personal survival metric. 'Not just the show, I mean you' is a great pivot — the tenderness of Jack's concern expressed as low expectation of her survival.

jokes.text: You're in an 'adult dude' situation. You're wearing a beautiful blazer from Rico's husky-boy collection... Is that what ragazzi robusti means?
jokes.setup: Jack is noting Liz's growth
jokes.punchline: Her 'beautiful blazer' is from the Rico's husky-boy collection — calling back to the blazer shop referenced earlier; Liz discovers what 'ragazzi robusti' means (robust/husky boys in Italian)
jokes.explanation: The Rico's callback pays off with a second joke — the Italian name for the shop translates to 'husky boys,' which Liz was wearing without knowing. Her dawning realization is a nice character moment layered onto the earlier gag.

jokes.text: Oh, my God. Hannibal defeated Fabian with a decoy army. James was a plant. The strie wall finish was a decoy. She hannibaled my Fabian!
jokes.setup: Liz asks if the wall removal might have been what Avery wanted all along
jokes.punchline: Jack realizes Avery outmaneuvered him entirely — she used her own Hannibal strategy against his Fabian strategy. 'She hannibaled my Fabian!' is the complete breakdown
jokes.explanation: The episode's thematic payoff — Jack's Fabian strategy, discussed throughout, is revealed to have been defeated by Avery's superior counter-strategy. 'She hannibaled my Fabian!' turns both historical generals into verbs, which is inventive language play. The structural elegance of the Fabian/Hannibal reversal is the episode's most complete joke — setup across 20 minutes, perfect payoff. Jack's horror at being out-strategized by his girlfriend is the character note that makes it sing.

jokes.text: Lemon, Avery and I are perfect together. Like... Whiskey and hunting. 'Soul mate' doesn't even begin to do it justice. She's my... She's your pube shirt. Pube shirt.
jokes.setup: Jack is searching for the right metaphor for his relationship with Avery
jokes.punchline: Liz completes it with 'pube shirt' — the would-you-rather garment from earlier is now the highest compliment in their shared vocabulary; Jack accepts it completely: 'Pube shirt.'
jokes.explanation: The episode's most satisfying callback. 'Pube shirt' — established as the thing you'd endure for love in the would-you-rather game — becomes the most romantic thing Jack can accept as a descriptor for Avery. 'She's my... Pube shirt.' spoken with complete sincerity by Jack Donaghy is formally beautiful. The callback transforms a gross absurdist joke into something almost moving. The best callback of the episode and one of 30 Rock's finest structural jokes.

jokes.text: Good night, TGS band, with your funny-smelling dressing room.
jokes.setup: The show wraps; Jenna does a theatrical good-night sign-off as producer
jokes.punchline: Her good night to the TGS band includes the parenthetical 'with your funny-smelling dressing room' — a specific, unglamorous detail that undercuts the formal farewell
jokes.explanation: A good small joke — Jenna's theatrical sign-off is deflated by the specific complaint about the band's smell. Characterful but not exceptional.

jokes.text: I lied to Mr. Jordan. I miss you all so much.
jokes.setup: Kenneth said his goodbyes earlier and appeared okay with leaving
jokes.punchline: Kenneth addresses the camera directly to reveal he lied to Tracy — he misses everyone deeply. The earnestness of the confession is both sweet and funny.
jokes.explanation: A touching button to the Kenneth storyline. The 'I lied' is the comedic element — he maintained composure for Tracy's sake and is now alone with his sadness. The humor comes from Kenneth's total sincerity in a slightly absurd framing.

jokes.text: Sir? Is it really you? Sure is. Wanna go kiss in the prop cage? What? No!
jokes.setup: Tracy sees someone at the end of the episode
jokes.punchline: Tracy immediately invites Brian to 'go kiss in the prop cage' — Brian's horrified refusal confirms this was a wildly inappropriate suggestion
jokes.explanation: A funny tag — Tracy's instant intimacy offer is startling and Brian's horror is the button. 'Prop cage' is a specific and funny location for the invitation. Ends the episode on an appropriately chaotic Tracy note.

tmdb_overview: Jack begins to meddle in Liz's new relationship with Carol.
insight: Season premiere reboots with 99 jokes in 24 minutes—peak joke density carries Liz through a reinvention arc.
